scenes.title: Typed Map Variables
scenes.narration: Last lesson the subnet map lived inside locals, and one field, N S G, was sitting unused. In this lesson that exact shape moves into its proper home: a typed input variable, fed by terraform dot t f vars. Same code, different data — the pattern every production Terraform codebase is built on.

for_each over the variable map, same loop as Lab 10
Outputs that report the layout: length() and keys()

scenes.narration: This is lab eleven, the assignment lab that follows directly from last lesson. The map of subnets doesn't live in locals anymore: it's now an input variable, and its values come from a separate file. That one move — data out of code — is what turns a teaching example into a reusable pattern.

scenes.heading: A type is a contract
points: map(object({ prefix = string, nsg = bool })): every value must match exactly
Wrong field names or wrong types → error before any plan runs
The .tfvars file is data; the .tf files are logic
Change the subnet layout by editing data only
scenes.narration: A map of object is more than a container: it's a contract. Every key maps to an object with exactly the fields declared here — a prefix string and an N S G boolean. Get the shape wrong, and Terraform rejects the file before any plan runs. That's the point: the code guarantees the data is sane, so the logic below can trust it completely.

scenes.narration: As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. Main dot t f, outputs dot t f, terraform dot t f, and — new since lab two — terraform dot t f vars, the data file this lesson is really about.

First the variable itself. Location is a plain string with a default. Subnets is the interesting one: a map of object, where every value must carry a prefix and an N S G flag. And notice — there's no default. The code refuses to guess a network layout. The data has to come from outside.

And here's the outside: terraform dot t f vars. Three keys — web, app, data — each an object with a prefix and an N S G flag, exactly the shape the variable demanded. Want a different layout for another environment? Edit this file and nothing else. Data changed, code untouched.

The resources are almost identical to last lesson. A resource group, a VNet, and one subnet resource with for each over the variable. Inside, each dot key names the subnet — s n e t, then the role — and each dot value dot prefix sets its address. The only thing that changed is where the map comes from.

scenes.caption: One variable, one layout — data drives the build
scenes.narration: Here's what the split looks like drawn out. The data file feeds a typed variable, and for each turns it into three subnets named after their roles. Edit the data, and the plan reshapes itself. The code never moves.

steps.narration: Here's what the split looks like drawn out.
Terraform dot t f vars is auto-loaded, its map lands in the typed variable, and for each turns it into three subnets.
Edit the data file — change a prefix, add a role — and the diff appears at plan time. The code never moved.
Each key becomes one subnet, named after the role it serves: web, app, and data.
One resource block, three instances — and the layout lives entirely in data.

scenes.narration: Two small outputs report the layout. Length counts the map entries, so subnet count is simply three. And keys lists the for each keys that became subnets — a quick, readable answer to the question, what did this configuration actually build?

Apply time. Five resources — group, VNet, and three subnets — all from one block plus one data file. The outputs confirm the shape: three entries, and the keys are the roles. Change the t f vars file and the next plan reshapes itself; the code stays exactly as it is.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — treating the type as loose guidance
points: tfvars must match map(object(...)) exactly — misspelled or missing fields are hard errors
The rejection happens before any plan — fail fast, by design
Keeping an unused field (nsg) in the shape is normal while a module grows
Adding a field later breaks every caller — design the shape up front
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: t f vars must match the map of object type exactly — misspelled or missing fields are hard errors. The type is a contract, not loose guidance; Terraform refuses the whole file before planning anything. Two: the rejection happens before any plan — fail fast, by design. A string where a boolean belongs dies in seconds on your machine instead of in the cloud. Three: keeping an unused field in the shape is normal while a module grows. The n s g flag is still riding along unused — that's deliberate. Four: adding a field later breaks every caller — design the shape up front. Add fields when you design, not when you deploy.

points: map(object({...})) is a shape-checked container — a contract, not a hint
terraform.tfvars supplies the data; main.tf holds the logic
for_each = var.subnets: same loop, data-driven source
length() and keys() report the built layout
Same code, different shapes per environment
scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: map of object is a shape-checked container — a contract, not a hint. Two: terraform dot t f vars supplies the data; main dot t f holds the logic. Three: for each over var dot subnets — the same loop, with a data-driven source. Four: length and keys report the built layout. Five: same code, different shapes per environment.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
